# Chapter 1: From Tough Coaches, Tough Parents, and Tough Guys to Finding Real Inner Strength

## The Old Model of Toughness

College students described toughness as "hard-nosed," "gritty," "playing through pain," "stoic," "persevering." Among 160 elite athletes, perseverance ranked highest. Traditional view: overcoming obstacles through perseverance, discipline, stoicism—often pictured as a strong brute of a man.

Bobby Knight exemplifies this. Over five decades: 900+ wins (third all-time), five Final Fours, three NCAA championships; his 1976 Indiana team went undefeated. Knight defined toughness as "being able to overcome obstacles. You can't feel sorry for yourself." His methods: hanging tampons from lockers of "soft" players; frequent cussing; a 1991 tirade ("This is absolute fucking bullshit. Now I'll fucking run your ass right into the ground"); bringing toilet paper with feces to show players what he thought of them; choking a player at practice. All in the name of toughness founded on showing no weakness, bulldozing obstacles, using fear to establish authority.

## Tough Parenting and Authoritarian Style

Developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind (1960s) classified parenting on two factors: responsiveness (attunement, support, fostering individuality) and demandingness (expectations, control, discipline). Three categories:
- **Permissive**: low demandingness, high responsiveness (too soft)
- **Authoritarian**: high demandingness, low responsiveness (too hard)
- **Authoritative**: high demandingness, high responsiveness (Goldilocks fit)

Authoritarian parents rely on fear, threats, punishment. Typical refrain: "You need to do (this) because I said so." In one study of over 1,000 parents, only 31% of authoritarian parents said they should "love their child unconditionally." Upon seeing a child miss a shot, they jump to criticism; ground kids after subpar test scores without support beyond "work harder." In another study, 81% of Americans thought parents were too soft. Same principles apply to coaching and leadership: we've taken demandingness and forgotten warmth, care, responsiveness.

## Callousness and Machismo

Language reveals confusion: teams called "soft," needing "hardening up"; "show no signs of weakness." In youth sports, children do burpees and laps to "toughen them up." In *Until It Hurts*, Mark Hyman found frequent vomiting after workouts and insult-laden tirades. Parents justified teaching eleven-year-olds to go until they puke: "The stern approach is necessary for children to get in touch with their inner lacrosse warrior."

Toughness tied to masculinity and machismo: "man up," "stop being a pussy," "There's no crying in baseball!" (*A League of Their Own*). Image is more The Rock or Vin Diesel than a small female of similar prowess. Yet women, who research shows quietly handle pain better than men, may have had the correct definition all along—based on reality, not false confidence and bluster.

## Consequences of the Callous View

On May 29, 2018, University of Maryland football player Jordan McNair (19) showed profound fatigue during ten 110-yard sprints. Coaches and trainers yelled "get him the [expletive] up" and "drag his [expletive] across the field." After McNair complained of cramps, it took trainers 34 minutes to get him off the field and another 28 minutes to call 911. He died two weeks later from heatstroke—partly due to inability to separate pushing through pain from actual danger.

Rhabdomyolysis, once rare, has become common due to extreme workouts designed not to improve fitness but to "test" athletes. As Ohio University professor B. David Ridpath described, the true notion is "to either toughen up the current players or weed out a few to open some scholarship slots."

Authoritarian parenting leads to lower independence, more aggression, higher substance abuse and risky behaviors. In sport: lower grit, increased emotional exhaustion, burnout, fear of failure. In one study of over 1,200 parents, authoritarian parenting linked to higher child misbehavior. Even in Israeli military, those from authoritarian environments coped worse than peers from nurturing environments. The style creates appearance of discipline without fostering it.

One young athlete explained: "Coaches use exercise as punishment because they want you to become stronger. It gets in your head and you start thinking, 'I need to do better. I need to work harder because I don't want to be punished.'" He worked to avoid punishment, not for internal reasons.

## Redefining Toughness

Fake toughness is control- and power-driven, developed through fear, fueled by insecurity, based on appearance over substance. It's Bobby Knight's tantrums, the bully at school, the executive who yells at subordinates, the strength coach whose athletes get injured. Real toughness is "experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It's maintaining a clear head to be able to make the appropriate decision."

Pete Carroll provides an alternative. After losing his NFL head coaching job in the 1990s, he stopped imitating others. He encourages meditation and yoga, shifts from meetings to ring toss if players get heated. One star player: "He's never negative, doesn't scream. He finds a way to turn a mistake into a positive." Carroll is one of only three coaches to win both an NCAA championship and a Super Bowl. He believes toughness comes from inner drive, embracing challenges, bouncing back. He replaces control with autonomy, appearance with substance, rigid pushing with flexibility, fear with inner drive, insecurity with quiet confidence.

Other successful coaches following this model: Don Shula, Bill Walsh, Tony Dungy (NFL); John Wooden, Dean Smith, Brad Stevens, Mike D'Antoni (basketball). D'Antoni told the author: "We keep it positive here." As Ken Reed (*Ego vs. Soul in Sports*) summarized: "For every Lombardi or Bobby Knight you give me, I can give you an equally successful—if not more successful—humanistic coach. Despite the success of Wooden, Shula, Dungy, Stevens, and others, our society has conditioned us to think that autocratic coaches are better coaches; that they win more often. It's a myth."

In 2008, researchers at Eastern Washington studied nearly 200 basketball players and their coaches, concluding: "The 'keys' to promoting mental toughness do not lie in this autocratic, authoritarian, or oppressive style. It appears to lie, paradoxically, with the coach's ability to produce an environment, which emphasizes trust and inclusion, humility, and service."

Real toughness provides the tool set to handle adversity. It's teaching, not fear. It pushes us to work with our body and mind, face reality, use feedback as information, accept emotions, develop a flexible array of responses. Navigating discomfort—anxiety, fear, pain, uncertainty, fatigue—means sometimes going through, around, under, or waiting until it passes. It requires many tools, not just a hammer.

## The Author's Personal Experience

The author describes racing the Don Bowden Mile at Cal. At 900 meters into the 1,609-meter race, he experienced a strange high-pitched gasp, as if his airway was blocked. He collapsed, unable to breathe. After a year of tests (scopes, echocardiograms, treadmill tests), allergist Dr. Stephen Miles diagnosed paradoxical vocal cord dysfunction (VCD)—the vocal cords shut when they should open, blocking inhalation. The American Thoracic Society cites "strong emotions" and stress as triggers. The author's usual strategy of pushing until he puked backfired. To continue running, he had to relax and keep his breathing, neck, and mind steady at the moment of highest discomfort. This search for what toughness really means became the foundation of the book.

The four pillars of real toughness:
1. Ditch the Facade, Embrace Reality
2. Listen to Your Body
3. Respond Instead of React
4. Transcend Discomfort

# Chapter 1: From Tough Coaches, Tough Parents, and Tough Guys to Finding Real Inner Strength

## The Old Model of Toughness

College students described toughness as "hard-nosed," "gritty," "playing through pain," "stoic," "persevering." Among 160 elite athletes, perseverance ranked highest. Traditional view: overcoming obstacles through perseverance, discipline, stoicism—often pictured as a strong brute of a man.

Bobby Knight exemplifies this. Over five decades: 900+ wins (third all-time), five Final Fours, three NCAA championships; his 1976 Indiana team went undefeated. Knight defined toughness as "being able to overcome obstacles. You can't feel sorry for yourself." His methods: hanging tampons from lockers of "soft" players; frequent cussing; a 1991 tirade ("This is absolute fucking bullshit. Now I'll fucking run your ass right into the ground"); bringing toilet paper with feces to show players what he thought of them; choking a player at practice. All in the name of toughness founded on showing no weakness, bulldozing obstacles, using fear to establish authority.

## Tough Parenting and Authoritarian Style

Developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind (1960s) classified parenting on two factors: responsiveness (attunement, support, fostering individuality) and demandingness (expectations, control, discipline). Three categories:
- **Permissive**: low demandingness, high responsiveness (too soft)
- **Authoritarian**: high demandingness, low responsiveness (too hard)
- **Authoritative**: high demandingness, high responsiveness (Goldilocks fit)

Authoritarian parents rely on fear, threats, punishment. Typical refrain: "You need to do (this) because I said so." In one study of over 1,000 parents, only 31% of authoritarian parents said they should "love their child unconditionally." Upon seeing a child miss a shot, they jump to criticism; ground kids after subpar test scores without support beyond "work harder." In another study, 81% of Americans thought parents were too soft. Same principles apply to coaching and leadership: we've taken demandingness and forgotten warmth, care, responsiveness.

## Callousness and Machismo

Language reveals confusion: teams called "soft," needing "hardening up"; "show no signs of weakness." In youth sports, children do burpees and laps to "toughen them up." In *Until It Hurts*, Mark Hyman found frequent vomiting after workouts and insult-laden tirades. Parents justified teaching eleven-year-olds to go until they puke: "The stern approach is necessary for children to get in touch with their inner lacrosse warrior."

Toughness tied to masculinity and machismo: "man up," "stop being a pussy," "There's no crying in baseball!" (*A League of Their Own*). Image is more The Rock or Vin Diesel than a small female of similar prowess. Yet women, who research shows quietly handle pain better than men, may have had the correct definition all along—based on reality, not false confidence and bluster.

## Consequences of the Callous View

On May 29, 2018, University of Maryland football player Jordan McNair (19) showed profound fatigue during ten 110-yard sprints. Coaches and trainers yelled "get him the [expletive] up" and "drag his [expletive] across the field." After McNair complained of cramps, it took trainers 34 minutes to get him off the field and another 28 minutes to call 911. He died two weeks later from heatstroke—partly due to inability to separate pushing through pain from actual danger.

Rhabdomyolysis, once rare, has become common due to extreme workouts designed not to improve fitness but to "test" athletes. As Ohio University professor B. David Ridpath described, the true notion is "to either toughen up the current players or weed out a few to open some scholarship slots."

Authoritarian parenting leads to lower independence, more aggression, higher substance abuse and risky behaviors. In sport: lower grit, increased emotional exhaustion, burnout, fear of failure. In one study of over 1,200 parents, authoritarian parenting linked to higher child misbehavior. Even in Israeli military, those from authoritarian environments coped worse than peers from nurturing environments. The style creates appearance of discipline without fostering it.

One young athlete explained: "Coaches use exercise as punishment because they want you to become stronger. It gets in your head and you start thinking, 'I need to do better. I need to work harder because I don't want to be punished.'" He worked to avoid punishment, not for internal reasons.

## Redefining Toughness

Fake toughness is control- and power-driven, developed through fear, fueled by insecurity, based on appearance over substance. It's Bobby Knight's tantrums, the bully at school, the executive who yells at subordinates, the strength coach whose athletes get injured. Real toughness is "experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It's maintaining a clear head to be able to make the appropriate decision."

Pete Carroll provides an alternative. After losing his NFL head coaching job in the 1990s, he stopped imitating others. He encourages meditation and yoga, shifts from meetings to ring toss if players get heated. One star player: "He's never negative, doesn't scream. He finds a way to turn a mistake into a positive." Carroll is one of only three coaches to win both an NCAA championship and a Super Bowl. He believes toughness comes from inner drive, embracing challenges, bouncing back. He replaces control with autonomy, appearance with substance, rigid pushing with flexibility, fear with inner drive, insecurity with quiet confidence.

Other successful coaches following this model: Don Shula, Bill Walsh, Tony Dungy (NFL); John Wooden, Dean Smith, Brad Stevens, Mike D'Antoni (basketball). D'Antoni told the author: "We keep it positive here." As Ken Reed (*Ego vs. Soul in Sports*) summarized: "For every Lombardi or Bobby Knight you give me, I can give you an equally successful—if not more successful—humanistic coach. Despite the success of Wooden, Shula, Dungy, Stevens, and others, our society has conditioned us to think that autocratic coaches are better coaches; that they win more often. It's a myth."

In 2008, researchers at Eastern Washington studied nearly 200 basketball players and their coaches, concluding: "The 'keys' to promoting mental toughness do not lie in this autocratic, authoritarian, or oppressive style. It appears to lie, paradoxically, with the coach's ability to produce an environment, which emphasizes trust and inclusion, humility, and service."

It pushes us to work with our body and mind, face reality, use feedback as information, accept emotions, develop a flexible array of responses. Navigating discomfort—anxiety, fear, pain, uncertainty, fatigue—means sometimes going through, around, under, or waiting until it passes. It requires many tools, not just a hammer.
